hook: The greatest mathematician of the ancient world, who shouted "Eureka!"

pages.x: Archimedes was born around 287 BC in Syracuse, a Greek city in Sicily, the son of an astronomer. He studied in Alexandria, then came home to serve King Hiero II. He grew so lost in his work that his servants had to drag him to the baths, where he drew shapes in the ashes of the fire.

Hiero suspected that his new gold crown had been mixed with silver. Stepping into a bath, Archimedes saw the water rise and realised he could measure the crown's volume by the water it pushed aside. He leapt out and ran home naked, shouting "Eureka!": "I have found it!"
He worked out the law of the lever and said: "Give me a place to stand, and I will move the Earth." His water screw, a spiral turning inside a tube, lifts water uphill.
pages.fx: Archimedes screws still pump water and move grain around the world, and his maths of levers and balance founded the science of mechanics.

pages.x: Using shapes with 96 sides, he showed that pi lies between 3 10/71 and 3 1/7, and that a sphere holds two thirds of the cylinder around it.
pages.fx: His methods came close to calculus, 1,900 years before Newton. He was so proud of the sphere result that he asked for it to be carved on his tomb.

pages.x: When Rome besieged Syracuse in 213 BC, his machines held it off for two years: catapults, and "the claw", a crane that lifted Roman ships out of the water and dropped them. A later legend says he set the fleet on fire with giant mirrors.

When the Romans finally took the city in 212 BC, a soldier found Archimedes drawing circles in the sand. "Do not disturb my circles," he said, and the soldier killed him. The Roman general, who had ordered that he be taken alive, was furious.

In 1906 a scholar in Constantinople found a medieval prayer book written over the scraped-off pages of works by Archimedes. X-ray imaging a century later revealed his lost book, The Method, which shows how he discovered his results.
Archimedes worked out why things float, how levers work and how to measure curved shapes, and came close to calculus. The Fields Medal, the top prize in mathematics, carries his portrait.
pts: Worked out the law of the lever
Measured pi and the volume of a sphere
Built war machines that held off Rome
